newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - U.S. vehicles roll off Russian assembly line.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. vehicles roll off Russian assembly line.

text.p: Thousands of miles from Detroit in the snowy wastes of a dilapidated industrial park, U.S. cars are rolling off a Russian assembly line.

"This is a victory -- I cannot call it anything else," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told workers in the semi-autonomous Russian region of Tatarstan who will assemble up to 10,000 Chevrolet Blazer sport utility vehicles from imported parts.
A full-scale assembly line, with an annual capacity for 45,000 vehicles, is due to to begin work towards the end of 1998.
U.S. carmaker General Motors has management control and a 25 percent equity stake in the $250-million joint venture Yelaz-GM, while the Russian and Tatar government share a 75 percent stake.
GM is ahead of Kia Motors Corp of South Korea and Volkswagen's Skoda unit in the race to assemble Western-style cars in Russia. The other two plan to start Russian assembly lines next year.
BIG MARKET POTENTIAL

The market potential is considered tremendous, with new car sales expected to grow to one to two million a year by the turn of the century. DRI/McGraw-Hill estimated new car sales this year at just under 700,000.
Yelaz-GM is built on top of a half-completed plant which the Soviet government first said would be used to build tractors, then for a 900,000-unit-a-year small car plant which was then abandoned.
The new GM assembly line is surrounded by more than 400 square km (155 square miles) of decaying Soviet buildings ravaged by the bitter Tatar wind and strung with icicles.
Marching from a light snowstorm into a warm assembly warehouse, presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais called the cars a model for industry.
"The licence plate should say "primer' (textbook), not "premier'," he joked, pointing at the back of the first vehicle, which Chernomyrdin took for a spin.

Russian manufacturers have been trying for years to lure foreign companies such as GM and Fiat into Russia, but none has accepted the challenge of working with existing Russian auto plants, which many view as overstaffed, poorly-financed, low-quality producers.
WORKING IN A FREE MARKET
Chubais and Chernomyrdin, speaking before the plant's formal opening on December 19, told Tatar industry leaders that they would have to make do without Moscow in the new free market.
"Aside from high marks, no one is going to give you anything," Chernomyrdin told the head of a local chemical concern.

The oil-rich Tatar republic agreed to finance construction of the Blazer plant with revenues from tax-exempt sales of crude oil, and GM officials say their chief risks are to the brand name and leaks of technology rather financial ones.
"Oil proceeds are financing the investment of the Yelaz-GM joint venture," said Greg DeYonker, executive vice-president of GM Overseas Corp and the GM executive in charge of the former Soviet Union.

High import duties push the legal price of an imported Blazer up to $65,000-$70,000, well beyond the reach of most Russians, and the large Jeep-type cars are often associated with shadowy criminal groups.
But the Russian-made models will face substantially lower tariffs and company officials said they could sell at around $25,000-$30,000.
Mikhail Tarasov, an assistant to Chernomyrdin, told Reuters that value added taxes on the Blazer would "at first be high", but gave no details. The VAT rate on automobiles is normally 20 percent.
RICH RUSSIANS CAN AFFORD COSTLY CARS

"We do not have to fight for the consumer now. There are rich people who can pay. Tomorrow, we need to make the car accessible for all," Tarasov said, adding that "a family car should be less than $20,000".
Russia is eager for tax revenues to help the economy spring to growth next year after a fall in gross domestic product of six percent in the 11 months to November to 1995.
David Dent, project manager for the Yelaz plant said the Blazer's affordability for its target customers -- young professionals and families -- would drop quickly as the price rose above $25,000.
"If it sells at $30,000, there are going to be a lot fewer customers buying that car than at $25,000," he said.

But Tarasov said Russia's economy should be growing at a brisk 4-5 percent per year by the time full production at the plant starts, which should increase affordability and help the government's ability to lower taxes.
DeYonker said Yelaz-GM dreamed of ultimately producing 250,000-300,000 cars a year, and GM had begun advanced planning on expanding the plant to build a passenger car.
This could begin by late 1999 under the right circumstances, he said. "We are dedicated to expanding that Blazer shop."
